title: Plasma, red cells and platelets
summary: Blood is a fluid tissue: plasma carrying three kinds of formed element.
objectives: State what plasma and the formed elements are and their rough proportions
Name the three main plasma proteins and where they are made
Describe an erythrocyte and a platelet: size, shape, count and lifespan
takeaways: Blood = plasma (~55%) + formed elements (~45%); plasma is ~91% water.
Albumins > globulins > fibrinogen; the liver makes albumin, fibrinogen and most clotting factors.
Red cells: ~5 million/mm³, anucleate biconcave discs ~7.5 µm, live ~120 days, removed by spleen and liver.
Platelets: 250,000–400,000/mm³, 2–4 µm fragments of megakaryocytes, for clotting.

steps.title: Plasma plus formed elements
steps.text:
Blood is a connective tissue whose matrix is a liquid, plasma. Spin a tube of blood and it separates: straw-coloured plasma on top (about 55%), a thin pale buffy coat of white cells and platelets, and packed red cells below (about 45%).

The cells and cell fragments are called the formed elements: erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets.

check.q: What are the three formed elements of blood?
check.a: Erythrocytes (red cells), leukocytes (white cells) and platelets.

steps.title: What plasma carries
steps.text:
Plasma is about 91% water. Most of the rest is protein: albumins (the largest share, made by the liver), globulins (second; some are antibodies made by plasma cells) and fibrinogen (the clotting protein, also from the liver). The liver makes most other clotting factors too.

The remainder is small solutes: electrolytes such as Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻, nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes.

check.q: Which plasma protein is most plentiful, and which organ makes it?
check.a: Albumin, made by the liver.

steps.title: Where blood cells are made
steps.text:
Hematopoiesis (hemopoiesis) is the making of blood cells. After birth it happens in red bone marrow, which in adults is found mainly in flat and irregular bones - sternum, ribs, vertebrae, hip bones - and the upper ends of the femur and humerus.

Erythropoiesis is the part of it that makes red cells.

check.q: What is the difference between hematopoiesis and erythropoiesis?
check.a: Hematopoiesis is formation of all blood cells; erythropoiesis is formation of red cells only.

steps.title: Erythrocytes
steps.text:
Red cells are by far the most numerous: about 5 million per mm³. Each is an anucleate, pink-staining biconcave disc about 7.5 µm across, paler in the middle. The dished shape gives a large surface area for oxygen exchange and lets the cell fold through capillaries.

Without a nucleus they cannot repair themselves: they live about 120 days and are then removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver.

check.q: Why is a red cell biconcave, and how long does it live?
check.a: The shape increases surface area for gas exchange (and flexibility); about 120 days.

steps.title: Platelets
steps.text:
Platelets (thrombocytes) are not whole cells but fragments pinched off giant megakaryocytes in the marrow. On a smear they are tiny purple specks, 2–4 µm, alone or in clumps, numbering 250,000–400,000 per mm³.

Their job is hemostasis: they stick at a damaged vessel, form a plug, and help the clotting cascade turn fibrinogen into a mesh of fibrin.

check.q: What cell do platelets come from?
check.a: The megakaryocyte of the red bone marrow.

practice.q: Roughly what fraction of plasma is water?
practice.why: Plasma is about 91% water; proteins make up about 7%.

practice.q: Which plasma protein is needed to form a clot?
practice.why: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin; like albumin it is made in the liver.

practice.q: Which plasma proteins include antibodies?
practice.why: Antibodies are immunoglobulins, a class of globulins made by plasma cells.

practice.q: Name three kinds of small solute carried in plasma.
practice.a: Electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻), nutrients, hormones, dissolved gases and wastes.

practice.q: Define hematopoiesis and say where it happens in an adult.
practice.a: The formation of blood cells (hemopoiesis), in red bone marrow.

practice.q: A normal red-cell count is about:
practice.why: About 5 million per mm³ - the most numerous formed element.

practice.q: How long does a red blood cell usually survive?
practice.why: About 120 days, after which the spleen and liver remove it.

practice.q: Describe an erythrocyte on a stained smear.
practice.a: A pink, anucleate biconcave disc about 7.5 µm across with a pale centre.

practice.q: Platelets are:
practice.why: They are anucleate fragments of megakaryocytes.

practice.q: What is the normal platelet count and their size?

title: White cells: the granulocytes
summary: How leukocytes leave the blood, and how to recognise a neutrophil, eosinophil and basophil.
objectives: Give the normal white-cell count and describe diapedesis and phagocytosis
Distinguish granulocytes from agranulocytes
Identify neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils and state what each does
takeaways: WBC ~7,000/mm³ (5,000–9,000); they leave capillaries by diapedesis and move by ameboid motion.
Granulocytes (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil) have granules and lobed nuclei (PMN).
Neutrophil 60–70%, multilobed, first-line phagocyte, up in acute bacterial infection.
Eosinophil 2–4%, red-orange granules, up in allergy and parasites; basophil 0.5–1%, histamine and heparin.

steps.title: Leukocytes work outside the blood
steps.text:
There are only about 7,000 white cells per mm³ (5,000–9,000). All are made in the bone marrow and live from hours to months. Blood is just their transport: they stick to the endothelium, squeeze out between the cells of capillary and venule walls (diapedesis) and crawl through tissue by ameboid movement.

Many then engulf bacteria and debris by phagocytosis.

check.q: What is diapedesis?
check.a: White cells squeezing out of a capillary or venule between its endothelial cells.

steps.title: Granulocytes and agranulocytes
steps.text:
On a Wright-stained smear white cells fall into two groups. Granulocytes have obvious cytoplasmic granules and a nucleus divided into lobes - hence 'polymorphonuclear' (PMN) leukocytes. They are the neutrophil, eosinophil and basophil.

Agranulocytes - lymphocytes and monocytes - show no visible granules and have a single unlobed nucleus.

check.q: Which three white cells are granulocytes?
check.a: Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.

steps.title: The neutrophil
steps.text:
The commonest white cell, 60–70% of the count. Its nucleus has 2–5 lobes joined by thin strands, and the cytoplasm holds fine, pale lilac granules that are hard to see. At 9–12 µm it is about 1.5 times a red cell.

Neutrophils live only 1–2 days and are the first phagocytes to reach infected tissue: their numbers rise in acute bacterial infection such as appendicitis.

check.q: Which white cell rises first in acute appendicitis?
check.a: The neutrophil.

steps.title: The eosinophil
steps.text:
Eosinophils make up 2–4%. The nucleus usually has two lobes, and the cytoplasm is packed with large red-orange granules - they love the acid dye eosin, hence the name. They are 10–14 µm, about twice a red cell.

They rise in allergic reactions and in parasitic worm infections, such as trichinosis from undercooked pork.

check.q: Name two conditions that raise the eosinophil count.
check.a: Allergies and parasitic (worm) infections such as trichinosis.

steps.title: The basophil
steps.text:
The rarest white cell, 0.5–1%, about 8–10 µm. Its coarse dark blue-purple granules crowd the cytoplasm and hide the bilobed nucleus.

The granules hold histamine, a vasodilator that makes vessels leaky, and heparin, an anticoagulant. Basophils increase in allergic and other inflammatory reactions.

check.q: Which two chemicals do basophil granules contain, and what does each do?
check.a: Histamine (vasodilator) and heparin (anticoagulant).

practice.q: A normal total white-cell count is about:
practice.why: About 7,000/mm³, range roughly 5,000–9,000.

practice.q: What is ameboid movement, and why do leukocytes need it?
practice.a: Crawling by extending the cytoplasm; it carries them through tissue after they leave the blood.

practice.q: A cell with 3–4 nuclear lobes and faint lilac granules is a:
practice.why: Multilobed nucleus with pale, fine granules is the neutrophil.

practice.q: Large red-orange granules and a bilobed nucleus identify a:
practice.why: Eosinophil granules take up eosin and stain red-orange.

practice.q: Which white cell releases histamine and heparin?
practice.why: Basophil granules contain histamine (vasodilator) and heparin (anticoagulant).

practice.q: What does 'polymorphonuclear leukocyte' refer to?
practice.a: Granulocytes, whose nucleus is divided into several lobes (especially neutrophils).

practice.q: Give the normal percentages of neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
practice.a: Neutrophils 60–70%, eosinophils 2–4%, basophils 0.5–1%.

practice.q: How long does a neutrophil typically live in the circulation?
practice.why: Neutrophils are short-lived: about 1–2 days.

practice.q: What is phagocytosis?
practice.a: Engulfing and digesting particles such as bacteria and debris.

title: Lymphocytes and monocytes
summary: The two agranulocytes: B and T lymphocytes that run specific immunity, and monocytes that become macrophages.
objectives: Identify a lymphocyte and a monocyte on a smear
Contrast B cells and antibody-mediated immunity with T cells and cell-mediated immunity
Name the organs where lymphocytes mature and gather
takeaways: Lymphocyte 20–25%: round dark nucleus with a thin rim of blue cytoplasm.
B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral immunity).
T cells mature in the thymus and attack infected, cancerous or transplanted cells directly.
Monocyte 3–8%, largest white cell, kidney-shaped nucleus; becomes a macrophage; up in chronic infection (TB).

steps.title: The lymphocyte
steps.text:
Lymphocytes make up 20–25% of white cells. Most are small - about a red cell's size - with a large, round or slightly dented, very dark nucleus surrounded by only a thin halo of pale blue cytoplasm; larger ones (up to ~17 µm) show more cytoplasm.

Their numbers rise in infections, especially viral ones, and in antigen–antibody reactions.

check.q: How do you recognise a lymphocyte?
check.a: A large round dark nucleus with only a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm and no granules.

steps.title: B cells: antibodies
steps.text:
B cells and T cells look identical on a stained smear. Both come from stem cells of the red bone marrow. B cells finish maturing in the marrow (in the fetus the liver and spleen also make them).

When a B cell meets its antigen it multiplies and becomes plasma cells, which secrete antibodies (immunoglobulins) into the blood. This is antibody-mediated, or humoral, immunity.

check.q: What does a B cell turn into, and what does that cell make?
check.a: A plasma cell, which secretes antibodies (immunoglobulins).

steps.title: T cells: cell-mediated immunity
steps.text:
T cells mature in the thymus, behind the upper sternum. Rather than making antibodies they act directly: they attack virus-infected cells, tumour cells and transplanted tissue. This is cell-mediated immunity.

T cells gather in the lymph nodes, thymus and spleen, and return to the blood through lymphatic vessels.

check.q: Where do T cells mature?
check.a: In the thymus.

steps.title: The monocyte
steps.text:
The largest white cell, 12–15 µm or more - about three red cells across - with plenty of grey-blue cytoplasm and a kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus. Monocytes are 3–8% of the count.

After a day or so in the blood they enter tissues and become macrophages, long-lived phagocytes. Monocytes rise in chronic infections such as tuberculosis.

check.q: What does a monocyte become once it enters the tissues?
check.a: A macrophage.

practice.q: Which white cell is the largest?
practice.why: Monocytes are 12–15 µm or more, about three red cells across.

practice.q: Plasma cells develop from:
practice.why: Activated B cells become antibody-secreting plasma cells.

practice.q: Cell-mediated immunity is carried out by:
practice.why: T cells attack virus-infected, tumour and transplanted cells directly.

practice.q: Another name for antibodies?
practice.a: Immunoglobulins.

practice.q: Contrast humoral and cell-mediated immunity.
practice.a: Humoral: B cells → plasma cells → antibodies in body fluids. Cell-mediated: T cells attack target cells directly.

practice.q: Monocytes rise characteristically in:
practice.why: Chronic infections such as tuberculosis raise the monocyte count.

practice.q: Give the normal percentages of lymphocytes and monocytes.
practice.a: Lymphocytes 20–25%; monocytes 3–8%.

practice.q: Can you tell a B cell from a T cell on a Wright-stained smear?
practice.a: No - they look identical.

practice.q: What is an antigen?
practice.a: A substance (usually foreign) that is recognised by and triggers a specific immune response.

title: The blood smear and the differential count
summary: How a smear is made and stained, and how the proportions of white cells point to disease.
objectives: Describe how a thin blood smear is made and stained
Explain how a differential white-cell count is done
Rank the white cells by abundance and link each rise to a cause
takeaways: A thin smear stained with Wright's (or Giemsa) stain is viewed under oil immersion.
Classify 100 white cells in a zig-zag scan; each count is then a percentage.
Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas: neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils.
Neutrophils ↑ acute bacterial; lymphocytes ↑ viral; monocytes ↑ chronic (TB); eosinophils ↑ allergy and parasites; basophils ↑ allergic inflammation.

steps.title: Making and staining a smear
steps.text:
A drop of blood from a fingertip puncture is spread into a thin film by drawing the edge of a second slide across it, so the cells lie one layer deep. Wright's stain (or Giemsa) combines the acid dye eosin, which colours red cells and eosinophil granules pink-orange, with basic dyes that turn nuclei purple.

Cells are examined at high power, usually under oil immersion. All blood is treated as a biohazard: sharps go in a sharps container.

check.q: What does eosin stain in a Wright-stained smear?
check.a: Red cells and eosinophil granules (pink to red-orange).

steps.title: Counting a hundred cells
steps.text:
A differential white-cell count classifies 100 consecutive leukocytes, so each tally is directly a percentage. The slide is moved in a zig-zag path across the thin part of the smear, so no field is counted twice and every region is sampled.

Red cells and platelets are ignored in this count; cell concentrations are given separately per mm³.

check.q: Why are exactly 100 cells counted?
check.a: So each count reads directly as a percentage of the white cells.

steps.title: The normal ranking
steps.text:
From most to least common: neutrophils 60–70%, lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 2–4% and basophils 0.5–1%.

Keep the three totals in mind too: red cells ~5 million/mm³, platelets 250,000–400,000/mm³, white cells ~7,000/mm³ - roughly one white cell for every 700 red cells.
steps.mnemonic: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas - Neutrophils, Lymphocytes, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils.

check.q: Rank the five white cells from most to least common.
check.a: Neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils.

steps.title: What a shift means
steps.text: Because each type has its own job, a change in the percentages points to a cause. Neutrophils rise in acute bacterial infection (appendicitis). Lymphocytes rise in viral infection. Monocytes rise in chronic infection such as tuberculosis. Eosinophils rise in allergy and parasitic infection (trichinosis). Basophils rise in allergic and inflammatory reactions.

check.q: A patient has 12% eosinophils. Name two likely causes.
check.a: An allergic reaction or a parasitic infection (e.g. trichinosis).

practice.q: Put the white cells in order of normal abundance, most first
Which stain is used for routine blood smears?
practice.why: Wright's (or Giemsa) stain - an eosin/basic-dye mixture.

practice.q: A differential count of 100 white cells finds 85 neutrophils. The most likely cause is:
practice.why: Neutrophilia points to acute bacterial infection such as appendicitis.

practice.q: Lymphocytosis most often suggests:
practice.why: Lymphocytes rise in viral infections and immune reactions.

practice.q: Why is the slide scanned in a zig-zag during a differential count?
practice.a: So no field is counted twice and the whole thin part of the smear is sampled.

practice.q: What objective is used to identify white cells on a smear?
practice.a: High power, usually oil immersion.

practice.q: Normal basophil percentage is:
practice.why: Basophils are the rarest white cell.

practice.q: What does 'cells per mm³' measure?
practice.a: The number of cells in one cubic millimetre of blood - a concentration, e.g. ~7,000 white cells/mm³.

practice.q: How should a used lancet and blood-stained materials be disposed of?
practice.a: Lancet in a sharps container; contaminated items into 10% bleach or a biohazard bag.

title: Where the heart sits and what wraps it
summary: The heart in the mediastinum, its apex and base on the chest wall, and the layers of the pericardium.
objectives: Describe the position of the heart and its neighbours in the mediastinum
Locate the apex and base of the heart on the chest wall
Name the layers of the pericardium and the pleura and the cavities between them
takeaways: The heart sits in the mediastinum, behind the sternum, in front of the thoracic vertebrae, on the diaphragm.
Base at the 2nd intercostal space; apex at the 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line.
Fibrous pericardium outside; serous pericardium = parietal layer + visceral layer (epicardium).
The pericardial cavity holds serous fluid that lets the heart beat with little friction.

steps.title: In the middle of the chest
steps.text:
The heart, about the size of a fist, lies in the mediastinum - the central compartment of the chest between the two lungs. It is behind the sternum, in front of the thoracic vertebrae, and rests on the diaphragm.

It shares the mediastinum with the oesophagus, the descending (thoracic) aorta, the trachea and the thymus. About two-thirds of it lies left of the midline.

check.q: Name three other structures that share the mediastinum with the heart.
check.a: Oesophagus, descending (thoracic) aorta, trachea (also thymus, great vessels).

steps.title: Apex and base on the chest wall
steps.text:
The heart is tipped: its broad base, where the great vessels attach, faces up, back and to the right, at about the level of the 2nd intercostal space. The pointed apex, formed by the left ventricle, points down, forward and left.

You can feel the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, in line with the middle of the left clavicle (the midclavicular line).

check.q: Where is the apex beat felt?
check.a: In the 5th left intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

steps.title: The pleura around the lungs
steps.text:
Each lung sits in its own serous sac. The visceral pleura clings to the lung surface; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. Between them is the pleural cavity, a slit holding a film of fluid.

The heart has exactly the same arrangement - a serous sac with a parietal and a visceral layer - called the pericardium.

check.q: Which layer of pleura lines the chest wall?
check.a: The parietal pleura.

steps.title: The pericardium
steps.text:
The outermost fibrous pericardium is a tough connective-tissue bag fused to the diaphragm; it anchors the heart and stops it overfilling. Inside it is the serous pericardium: a parietal layer lining the fibrous bag, folding back at the great vessels as the visceral layer (epicardium) on the heart itself.

Between the two is the pericardial cavity, with a little serous fluid that reduces friction.

check.q: What is another name for the visceral pericardium?
check.a: The epicardium.

practice.q: The apex of the heart lies at the:
practice.why: The apex beat is in the 5th left intercostal space.

practice.q: From outside in, the correct order is:
choices: Fibrous pericardium, parietal layer, pericardial cavity, visceral layer
Parietal layer, fibrous pericardium, visceral layer, cavity
Visceral layer, cavity, parietal layer, fibrous pericardium
Fibrous pericardium, visceral layer, cavity, parietal layer
practice.why: The fibrous sac is lined by the parietal serous layer; the cavity separates it from the visceral layer.

practice.q: What is the mediastinum?
practice.a: The central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs.

practice.q: What is the function of serous pericardial fluid?
practice.a: It lubricates, reducing friction as the heart beats.

practice.q: Where is the base of the heart?
practice.a: Superior-posterior, where the great vessels attach - about the level of the 2nd intercostal space.

practice.q: Order the layers from the chest wall to the lung

title: The heart wall and cardiac muscle
summary: Epicardium, myocardium and endocardium, and the branching, striated cells that make the wall pump.
objectives: Name the three layers of the heart wall and the tissue of each
Describe cardiac muscle cells and intercalated discs
Explain why the ventricles wring rather than simply squeeze
takeaways: Epicardium: simple squamous mesothelium over loose connective tissue and fat (coronary vessels run here).
Myocardium: the thick cardiac muscle layer.
Endocardium: endothelium on thin connective tissue, lining the chambers and covering the valves.
Cardiac cells are striated, branched and joined at intercalated discs; spiral bundles wring blood out.

steps.title: Three layers
steps.text:
The epicardium is the visceral pericardium: a simple squamous mesothelium over loose connective tissue and fat, in which the coronary vessels run. The myocardium, by far the thickest layer, is cardiac muscle. The endocardium is an endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) on a thin connective-tissue layer; it lines the chambers, covers the valves and is continuous with the lining of the vessels.

In the heart model the three layers are separate parts: the epicardium with its epicardial fat, the ventricular myocardium and the endocardium. The two thin layers are drawn thicker than life.

check.q: Which layer of the heart wall is thickest?
check.a: The myocardium.

steps.title: Cardiac muscle cells
steps.text:
Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but its cells are short, branched and usually have one central nucleus. Neighbouring cells join end to end at intercalated discs, dark cross-bands packed with gap junctions and desmosomes.

The gap junctions let the impulse pass straight from cell to cell, so the whole chamber contracts as one unit. In the model, switch to the Teased state to pull one cell back and open a disc.
micro_focus: Cardiomyocyte 21 (partner cell of the hero disc)

check.q: What are intercalated discs and why do they matter?
check.a: Junctions between cardiac cells, with gap junctions that pass the impulse so the muscle contracts as a unit.

steps.title: A wringing pump
steps.text:
The ventricular muscle is laid down in spiral bundles that wind around the chambers. When they shorten, the ventricle twists and wrings blood from the apex up toward the outflow valves, rather than just squeezing it.

The inner surface of the ventricles is not smooth but raised into muscular ridges, the trabeculae carneae. The left ventricular wall is much thicker than the right.

check.q: What are trabeculae carneae?
check.a: Muscular ridges on the inner wall of the ventricles.

practice.q: What lines the inside of the heart chambers, and what kind of tissue is it?
practice.a: The endocardium: an endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) on a thin connective-tissue layer, continuous with the lining of the vessels.

practice.q: Order the tissues of the heart wall from the outside in
Order the layers of the heart wall from outside in
The endocardium is made mainly of:
practice.why: Endocardium = endothelium (simple squamous) over a thin connective-tissue layer.

practice.q: Which feature is found in cardiac but not skeletal muscle?
practice.why: Intercalated discs join cardiac cells end to end.

practice.q: What tissue forms the epicardium?
practice.a: Simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium) over loose connective tissue and adipose tissue.

practice.q: Why does the spiral arrangement of myocardium matter?
practice.a: Contraction wrings the ventricle, pushing blood from apex toward the outflow valves.

title: Chambers and the path of blood
summary: Four chambers, two circuits: trace a drop of blood from the venae cavae back to the aorta.
objectives: Name the four chambers and say which receive and which pump
Trace blood through the heart, valves and pulmonary and systemic circuits in order
Explain why pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood and why the left ventricle is thicker
takeaways: Atria receive (thin walls, auricles); ventricles pump.
Venae cavae/coronary sinus → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary trunk → lungs.
Pulmonary veins → LA → bicuspid → LV → aortic valve → aorta → body.
Arteries leave the heart, veins return to it - whatever their oxygen content.

steps.title: Four chambers, two pumps
steps.text:
The two atria sit above and behind: thin-walled receiving chambers, each with an ear-shaped pouch, the auricle. The two ventricles below are the thick-walled pumping chambers.

The right atrium and ventricle pump to the lungs; the left atrium and ventricle pump to the rest of the body. The right ventricle forms most of the front of the heart.

check.q: Which chambers receive blood and which pump it out?
check.a: Atria receive; ventricles pump.

steps.title: Right heart to the lungs
steps.text: Deoxygenated blood returns through the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus into the right atrium. It passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary trunk. The trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries to the lungs, where blood gives up CO₂ and picks up O₂.

check.q: Which valve does blood pass on leaving the right ventricle?
check.a: The pulmonary semilunar valve.

steps.title: Left heart to the body
steps.text:
Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs in four pulmonary veins into the left atrium. It passes the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta and so to every tissue of the body.

From the tissues it returns, deoxygenated, to the venae cavae and the cycle repeats.

check.q: Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?
check.a: The bicuspid (mitral) valve.

steps.title: Two circuits and a naming trap
steps.text:
The pulmonary circuit runs from the right ventricle to the left atrium; the systemic circuit from the left ventricle to the right atrium. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins toward it, so the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins oxygenated blood.

The left ventricle drives the high-pressure systemic circuit, so its wall is about three times thicker than the right's.
steps.pitfall: 'Artery' means away from the heart, not 'oxygenated'. The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries after birth that carry deoxygenated blood.

check.q: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker than the right?
check.a: It must generate the much higher pressure needed to drive the systemic circulation.

practice.q: Trace blood from the venae cavae to the aorta
Which vessels carry oxygenated blood?
practice.why: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practice.q: Which three vessels empty into the right atrium?
choices: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, coronary sinus
Superior vena cava and pulmonary veins
practice.why: Both venae cavae and the coronary sinus drain into the right atrium.

practice.q: What happens to blood in the lungs?
practice.a: It releases CO₂ and picks up O₂.

practice.q: What are the auricles?
practice.a: Ear-like flaps (pouches) extending from each atrium.

practice.q: Define the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
practice.a: Pulmonary: right ventricle → lungs → left atrium. Systemic: left ventricle → body → right atrium.

title: Outside the heart: grooves and coronary vessels
summary: The apex, base and sulci of the heart, and the arteries and veins that run in them.
objectives: Identify the apex, base, great vessels and ligamentum arteriosum on the heart's surface
Name the three sulci and what runs in each
Trace the coronary arteries and cardiac veins and explain when the coronaries fill
takeaways: Coronary (AV) sulcus: RCA, circumflex, coronary sinus. Anterior IV sulcus: anterior interventricular artery + great cardiac vein. Posterior IV sulcus: posterior interventricular artery + middle cardiac vein.
LCA → anterior interventricular + circumflex (→ left marginal). RCA → right marginal + posterior interventricular.
Cardiac veins → coronary sinus → right atrium.
Coronary arteries fill mainly during ventricular relaxation (diastole).

steps.title: Apex, base and the great vessels
steps.text:
The pointed apex is formed by the left ventricle. At the base the great vessels leave: the pulmonary trunk in front, and the aorta behind it, arching up and to the left over the pulmonary arteries.

A short fibrous cord, the ligamentum arteriosum, joins the pulmonary trunk to the underside of the aortic arch. It is the remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus; a small lymph node usually sits beside it.

check.q: What is the ligamentum arteriosum a remnant of?
check.a: The fetal ductus arteriosus.

steps.title: Three grooves
steps.text: The coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus encircles the heart between atria and ventricles; it carries the right coronary artery, the circumflex artery and, behind, the coronary sinus. The anterior interventricular sulcus marks the septum between the ventricles on the front and holds the anterior interventricular artery and great cardiac vein. The posterior interventricular sulcus holds the posterior interventricular artery and middle cardiac vein.

check.q: What runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus?
check.a: The anterior interventricular artery and the great cardiac vein.

steps.title: The coronary arteries
steps.text:
The left and right coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve. The left divides at once into the anterior interventricular artery (the LAD) and the circumflex artery, which runs left in the coronary sulcus and gives the left marginal artery.

The right runs right in the coronary sulcus, giving the right marginal artery and the posterior interventricular artery.

check.q: What are the two main branches of the left coronary artery?
check.a: The anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery.

steps.title: Filled between beats
steps.text:
When the ventricles contract (systole) the muscle squeezes the arteries running through it, so coronary blood flow happens mainly while the ventricles relax (diastole). A fast heart rate shortens diastole and so shortens the heart's own blood supply.

The vessels are ordinary muscular arteries - intima, media, adventitia - and so are prone to narrowing by plaque. The muscular-artery model shows the three layers of such a wall.

check.q: When do the coronary arteries receive most of their flow?
check.a: During ventricular relaxation (diastole).

steps.title: The cardiac veins
steps.text:
The great cardiac vein climbs the anterior interventricular sulcus and turns left into the coronary sulcus. The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular sulcus, the small cardiac vein along the right margin, and the posterior vein of the left ventricle up its back.

All empty into the coronary sinus, a wide channel in the back of the coronary sulcus that opens into the right atrium.

check.q: Where does the coronary sinus empty?
check.a: Into the right atrium.

practice.q: The coronary sinus lies in the:
choices: Posterior part of the coronary sulcus
practice.why: It runs in the back of the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and opens into the right atrium.

practice.q: The posterior interventricular artery usually arises from the:
practice.why: It is normally a branch of the right coronary artery.

practice.q: Which vein accompanies the anterior interventricular artery?
practice.why: The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus.

practice.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
practice.a: From the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve - the first branches of the aorta.

practice.q: Why is coronary flow greatest during diastole?
practice.a: In systole the contracting myocardium compresses the vessels within it.

practice.q: Trace venous blood from the front of the left ventricle to the right atrium

title: Inside the heart: septa and valves
summary: The walls between the chambers, the fossa ovalis, and the four valves with their cords and muscles.
objectives: Identify the interatrial and interventricular septa, fossa ovalis, pectinate muscles and trabeculae carneae
Describe the atrioventricular valves with their chordae tendineae and papillary muscles
Explain how the semilunar valves open and close
takeaways: Fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum = remnant of the fetal foramen ovale.
Pectinate muscles ridge the atria/auricles; trabeculae carneae ridge the ventricles.
Tricuspid (right AV, 3 cusps) and bicuspid/mitral (left AV, 2 cusps) stop backflow into the atria in systole; chordae tendineae and papillary muscles stop the cusps everting.
Pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves (3 cusps each) stop backflow into the ventricles in diastole.

steps.title: The septa and the atrial walls
steps.text:
The interatrial septum divides the atria. On its right side is a shallow oval dip, the fossa ovalis - all that remains of the foramen ovale, a fetal opening that closes after birth. The thick interventricular septum divides the ventricles.

Parallel ridges, the pectinate muscles, line the auricles and front of the atria; the ventricles are lined by the irregular trabeculae carneae.

check.q: What is the fossa ovalis?
check.a: A depression in the interatrial septum, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale.

steps.title: The atrioventricular valves
steps.text:
Each atrium opens into its ventricle through an atrioventricular canal guarded by an AV valve. The right one, the tricuspid valve, has three cusps. The left one, the bicuspid (mitral) valve, has two.

They open when the atria fill the ventricles, and close as the ventricles contract, stopping blood being pushed back into the atria.
focus: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve
steps.pitfall: The atlas group 'right atrioventricular valve' also pulls in a left-sided leaflet - use the named leaflets instead.

check.q: How many cusps does the mitral valve have?
check.a: Two - it is the bicuspid valve.

steps.title: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles
steps.text:
The free edges of the AV cusps are tethered by fine tendinous cords, the chordae tendineae, to cone-shaped papillary muscles projecting from the ventricular wall.

The papillary muscles contract with the ventricle and pull the cords tight, so the cusps meet and are not blown back (everted) into the atria like an umbrella in the wind.
focus: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal papillary muscle of right ventricle
Inferior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle

check.q: What stops the AV valve cusps being pushed into the atria?
check.a: Chordae tendineae held taut by contracting papillary muscles.

steps.title: The semilunar valves
steps.text: The pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves each have three half-moon pocket-shaped cusps and no cords. When the ventricles eject, blood flattens the cusps against the vessel wall. When the ventricles relax, blood falls back, fills the pockets and snaps them shut - preventing backflow from the arteries into the ventricles.

check.q: When do the semilunar valves close?
check.a: When the ventricles relax (start of diastole) and blood falls back toward them.

practice.structure: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle

practice.q: The tricuspid valve lies between the:
practice.why: The tricuspid is the right atrioventricular valve.

practice.q: Which valves have chordae tendineae?
practice.why: Only the AV valves are tethered to papillary muscles by chordae.

practice.q: Pectinate muscles are found in the:
practice.why: Pectinate muscles ridge the atrial walls; trabeculae carneae ridge the ventricles.

practice.q: What does a semilunar valve prevent?
practice.a: Backflow from the artery into the ventricle during ventricular relaxation.

title: The sheep heart, mapped to the human
summary: A sheep heart is a good stand-in for ours: how its vessels and chambers correspond.
objectives: Match the sheep heart's venae cavae and great vessels to the human names
Tell the anterior from the posterior surface and the right from the left ventricle
Describe what a section through the interventricular septum shows
takeaways: Anterior vena cava = superior vena cava; posterior vena cava = inferior vena cava.
The pulmonary trunk is the most anterior vessel and leads to the right ventricle; the aorta lies behind it and leads to the left ventricle.
The coronary sinus opens in the posterior, inferior right atrium; pulmonary veins enter the left atrium.
A coronal cut through the interventricular septum opens all four chambers.

steps.title: Same plan, different names
steps.text:
A sheep's heart has the same four chambers, valves and vessels as ours. Because the animal stands on four legs, its superior vena cava is called the anterior vena cava and its inferior vena cava the posterior vena cava.

It usually carries a thick layer of epicardial fat, which fills the sulci and hides the coronary vessels.

check.q: What is the human name for the sheep's posterior vena cava?
check.a: Inferior vena cava.

steps.title: Front, back, right and left
steps.text:
The anterior surface is recognised by the anterior interventricular sulcus running diagonally toward the apex. The pulmonary trunk is the most anterior vessel and leaves toward the specimen's left; a blunt probe passed down it enters the right ventricle. The aorta lies directly behind it and leads to the left ventricle.

Squeeze the ventricles: the left is firm and thick-walled, the right softer.

check.q: Which ventricle does the pulmonary trunk lead into?
check.a: The right ventricle.

steps.title: The openings into the atria
steps.text:
Both venae cavae open into the right atrium; the coronary sinus opens in its posterior, inferior part near the inferior vena cava. The pulmonary veins enter the left atrium on the back of the heart - often seen as four veins, sometimes as two openings when they merge.

The atrial walls are thin enough to feel a probe through them.

check.q: Where does the coronary sinus open?
check.a: Into the posterior, inferior right atrium.

steps.title: The four-chamber cut
steps.text: A coronal cut from apex to base through the interventricular septum opens all four chambers at once. It shows the thin atrial walls, the thick left and thinner right ventricular walls, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves with their chordae and papillary muscles, the trabeculae carneae and the septa - the same view as the cut-away of the heart model.

check.q: Why cut through the interventricular septum?
check.a: The plane passes through all four chambers and both AV valves at once.

practice.q: In a sheep, the anterior vena cava corresponds to the human:
practice.why: Anterior (cranial) in a quadruped = superior in an upright human.

practice.q: A probe passed down the aorta enters the:
practice.why: The aorta leaves the left ventricle.

practice.q: Why are the coronary vessels hard to see on a sheep heart?
practice.a: They lie in the sulci buried in a thick layer of epicardial fat.

practice.q: How can you tell the left ventricle from the right by touch?
practice.a: The left ventricle's wall is much thicker and firmer.
